candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.source_attribution: 1 Enoch 6:1-2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Tewahedo canonical text (Mäṣḥafä Hēnok).
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'It came to pass when the children of men had multiplied that in those days were born unto them beautiful and comely daughters. And the angels, the children of the heaven, saw and lusted after them' — the foundational Watcher narrative that expands Genesis 6:1-4. Two hundred angels under Semjâzâ descend on Mount Hermon and bind themselves by oath to take human wives, knowing the act is forbidden. The Tewahedo reading takes this not as mythological folklore but as actual cosmic-historical rebellion: the disordering of the angelic order is the proximate cause of the disordering of the human order that necessitates the Flood. This is the Tewahedo canonical anchor that distinguishes its angelology from those of other Christian traditions.

candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'And the angels, the children of the heaven, saw and lusted after them, and said to one another: Come, let us choose us wives from among the children of men and beget us children' — the deliberate-collective character of the Watchers' decision. The rebellion is not impulsive individual passion but coordinated council: 'said to one another' frames the sin as conspiratorial, not accidental. The Tewahedo angelological tradition reads this against any reading that would minimize Satan-and-the-fallen-angels as mere temptation-creatures: they are genuine moral agents with developed plans, not impulsive nature-spirits.

candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'Then sware they all together and bound themselves by mutual imprecations upon it' — the angelic oath that seals the rebellion. The mutual binding-by-oath ensures no individual angel can retreat from the collective plan: each is now bound to all the others. Tewahedo demonological tradition reads this as the prototype of every subsequent secret-society oath: the binding-by-mutual-imprecation is the demonic technology for ensuring collective evil endures past individual second-thoughts. The verse warrants a deep ascetic suspicion of any oath-bound association outside the Church's sacramental order.

candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.source_attribution: 1 Enoch 6:1-2, trans. R.H. Charles (1912). PD. Tewahedo canonical text (Mäṣḥafä Hēnok).
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'It came to pass when the children of men had multiplied that in those days were born unto them beautiful and comely daughters. And the angels, the children of the heaven, saw and lusted after them' — the foundational Watcher narrative that expands Genesis 6:1-4. Two hundred angels under Semjâzâ descend on Mount Hermon and bind themselves by oath to take human wives, knowing the act is forbidden. The Tewahedo reading takes this not as mythological folklore but as actual cosmic-historical rebellion: the disordering of the angelic order is the proximate cause of the disordering of the human order that necessitates the Flood. This is the Tewahedo canonical anchor that distinguishes its angelology from those of other Christian traditions.

candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'And the angels, the children of the heaven, saw and lusted after them, and said to one another: Come, let us choose us wives from among the children of men and beget us children' — the deliberate-collective character of the Watchers' decision. The rebellion is not impulsive individual passion but coordinated council: 'said to one another' frames the sin as conspiratorial, not accidental. The Tewahedo angelological tradition reads this against any reading that would minimize Satan-and-the-fallen-angels as mere temptation-creatures: they are genuine moral agents with developed plans, not impulsive nature-spirits.

candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'Then sware they all together and bound themselves by mutual imprecations upon it' — the angelic oath that seals the rebellion. The mutual binding-by-oath ensures no individual angel can retreat from the collective plan: each is now bound to all the others. Tewahedo demonological tradition reads this as the prototype of every subsequent secret-society oath: the binding-by-mutual-imprecation is the demonic technology for ensuring collective evil endures past individual second-thoughts. The verse warrants a deep ascetic suspicion of any oath-bound association outside the Church's sacramental order.

candidates.source_name: 1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36)
candidates.draft_body:
1 Enoch (Ethiopian tradition) Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1-36) (c. 200 BC)

'And they were in all two hundred; who descended in the days of Jared on the summit of Mount Hermon' — the precise location and numbering of the Watchers' descent. Mount Hermon in northern Israel (the headwaters of the Jordan) becomes for the Tewahedo tradition the geographical inverse of Mount Sinai: Sinai is where God descends to give the Law; Hermon is where the rebellious angels descend to disorder creation. The Mäṣḥafä Hēnok dating in the days of Jared (Enoch's father) places the rebellion seven generations after Adam — the moral entropy of the post-fall world accelerating until Noah.
